code.title: Class vs struct: copy and equality behaviour

followUps:
A struct hurts when it is large or copied a lot, because every assignment, argument pass and return copies all its bytes. A struct of 40 bytes passed through 5 calls is copied 5 times, while a class passes one 8-byte reference.

It also hurts when it is boxed (cast to object or an interface), when it is used as a dictionary key without IEquatable<T>, and when it is mutable, since changes land on temporary copies. Keep structs at about 16 bytes, immutable, and pass big ones with in. Measure before choosing.

No, records are only shallowly immutable: the properties cannot be reassigned, but whatever they point to can still change.

A record Team(string Name, List<string> Members) blocks t.Members = x, yet t.Members.Add("Bob") works. Equality also compares the list by reference, so two teams with identical members are not equal. Use ImmutableArray<T> or copy the input, and a with expression copies only the top level.

code.title: Value copies, ref parameters and boxing

followUps:
Boxing is wrapping a value type in a new heap object so it can be used as an object or interface; it allocates and copies the value.

It happens implicitly when you pass an int to a parameter of type object, use non-generic collections like ArrayList, call string.Format("{0}", 5), put a struct in an interface variable, or use a struct as a key without IEquatable<T>. One box of an int is about 24 bytes of garbage, so in a loop of a million iterations it costs about 24 MB. Generics avoid it.

in passes an argument by readonly reference, so a large struct is not copied and the method cannot assign to it.

Example: double Dist(in Vec3 a, in Vec3 b) reads the caller's two structs directly instead of copying 24 bytes each. The caller does not need to write in. Pitfall: calling a non-readonly method on an in struct makes the compiler create a defensive copy, so mark the struct readonly struct. For small structs (up to 16 bytes) plain by-value is as fast.

code.title: Immutable type with defensive copy and With method

followUps:
ImmutableArray<T> is a thin wrapper over an array: very fast reads and low memory, but every change copies the whole array. ImmutableList<T> is a balanced tree: reads are slower, but a change copies only about log N nodes.

With 1,000 items, reading by index is O(1) for the array and O(log N) (around 10 steps) for the list; adding one item is O(N), around 1,000 copies, for the array and around 10 node allocations for the list. Build once and read often: use ImmutableArray. Many small updates to a big collection: ImmutableList.

Keep the whole state in one immutable object and swap a single reference to publish a new version; readers never see a half-updated state.

volatile Config current = new Config(...);
// writer
current = current.With(timeout: 30);
// readers
var snap = current; // use snap consistently

Reference writes are atomic. If several writers update from the old value, use Interlocked.CompareExchange in a loop, or ImmutableInterlocked.Update, so none of the updates is lost.

code.title: Result type versus exceptions for expected failures

followUps:
Run each check separately, keep every failure, and combine them at the end, so the user sees all problems at once instead of only the first.

Example: name empty, age -3 and email bad should give 3 errors, not 1. With Bind the chain stops at the first failure, so use a different combinator that collects errors:

var errors = new List<string>();
if (name == "") errors.Add("name required");
if (age < 0) errors.Add("age must be >= 0");
return errors.Count == 0 ? Ok(new User(name, age)) : Fail(errors);

Independent checks collect errors (applicative style); dependent steps chain with Bind.

Map each error kind to a status code in one place, usually at the edge of the web layer, so the domain code stays free of HTTP.

Typical mapping: validation errors become 400 (with the list of messages), not found becomes 404, a conflict such as a duplicate becomes 409, an unexpected failure stays an exception and becomes 500. Give errors a code or type (an enum like NotFound) rather than matching on message text, then write one switch that turns Result into IActionResult and reuse it in every endpoint.

code.title: Dispose pattern with idempotent Dispose

followUps:
SafeHandle is a .NET base class that wraps an operating system handle and guarantees it is released, even when the program is shutting down or a thread is aborted.

It has a built-in critical finalizer and a reference count, so the handle cannot be freed while a native call is still using it, and it protects against handle recycling attacks. You write class MyHandle : SafeHandleZeroOrMinusOneIsInvalid and override ReleaseHandle(). Your own class then holds a SafeHandle field and just implements Dispose, without a finalizer of its own.

The DI container disposes the services it created, when their scope ends; you must not dispose them yourself.

Singletons are disposed when the root provider is disposed (app shutdown), scoped services when the scope ends (in ASP.NET Core, at the end of the request), and transient services are disposed with the scope that resolved them, so a transient resolved from the root lives until shutdown. Objects you create with new, or registered as an existing instance (AddSingleton(instance)), are not disposed by the container; you own them.

code.title: Task.WhenAll rethrows only one exception

followUps:
It is still useful in library code that has no need to return to the caller's context, because it avoids the cost of posting back and the risk of deadlock when someone blocks on your task.

In ASP.NET Core there is no synchronization context, so it changes nothing there. In UI apps (WPF, WinForms, MAUI) code after await must return to the UI thread to touch controls, so application code keeps the default, while a reusable library should use ConfigureAwait(false) on every await. It saves about one thread hop per await.

Look for symptoms first: requests getting slower while CPU stays low, and the thread pool queue growing instead of work finishing.

Tools: dotnet-counters (watch ThreadPool Queue Length and Thread Count; a count climbing by about 1 or 2 threads per second is the pool injecting threads to cope), dotnet-stack or a dump to see many threads parked in .Result or .Wait(), and ThreadPool.GetAvailableThreads in a health check. The fix is to remove the blocking calls, not to raise the minimum thread count.

code.title: Equals without GetHashCode and mutable keys in a HashSet

followUps:
Because an attacker who can choose keys could otherwise craft many strings with the same hash, making a dictionary slow (about N times N work for N keys) and causing a denial of service.

.NET seeds string hashing with a random value chosen at process start, so the same string has a different hash on each run. Consequence: never store GetHashCode() in a file or database, and never compare hashes between machines or runs. Use a stable hash such as SHA-256 or a hand-written FNV for persistent values.

Write the record's Equals and GetHashCode yourself, comparing the array contents, because the generated ones compare the array by reference.

record Data(int[] Items) {
  public virtual bool Equals(Data? o) => o != null && Items.SequenceEqual(o.Items);
  public override int GetHashCode() { var h = new HashCode(); foreach (var i in Items) h.Add(i); return h.ToHashCode(); }
}

Alternatively store an ImmutableArray wrapper type that has structural equality, so the record stays automatic.

code.title: LINQ deferred execution runs the query again each time

followUps:
An iterator method (one using yield return) is deferred execution written by hand: the compiler turns it into a state machine and no line of the body runs until the first MoveNext().

Example: IEnumerable<int> Gen() { Console.WriteLine("start"); yield return 1; }. Calling var g = Gen(); prints nothing; foreach prints "start". So argument checks inside an iterator fire late; split into a public method that validates and a private iterator that yields.

CA1851 warns about possible multiple enumeration of an IEnumerable: the same lazy query is looped over more than once.

For var q = items.Where(Slow); var n = q.Count(); var f = q.First(); the filter runs twice and any database call behind it runs twice. The fix is var list = items.Where(Slow).ToList(); and then using list, or taking IReadOnlyCollection<T> as the parameter type to say that the data is already materialised.

code.title: Closures capture variables: for loop bug and fix

followUps:
Give each iteration its own variable by copying the loop variable into a local declared inside the loop body, or use foreach.

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    int copy = i;            // new variable each pass
    actions.Add(() => Console.WriteLine(copy));
}

Without the copy all three lambdas share one i that ends at 3, so they print 3 3 3; with it they print 0 1 2. The compiler then creates one closure object per iteration (3 small allocations).

A static lambda is not allowed to capture anything from the surrounding method, which the compiler enforces, so it can never allocate a closure.

Writing list.Select(static x => x * 2) compiles, but static x => x * factor is an error if factor is a local. It documents intent and protects a hot path from an accidental capture. If you need data, pass it through a state parameter, for example an overload that takes (state, x).

code.title: Allocating garbage versus reusing a buffer

followUps:
The mid-life crisis is when objects live long enough to be promoted to gen1 or gen2 and then die soon after, which makes the GC do expensive work for them.

Gen0 collections are cheap because almost everything is already dead; gen2 collections must scan a lot of the heap. Objects that survive a few collections, such as cache entries or request data held for a few seconds, get copied and promoted, then die in gen2 and need a full collection to be cleaned. Avoid it by freeing objects quickly, pooling them, or keeping them truly long-lived.

Use Server GC for a server application that has many cores and needs high throughput, such as a web API on a dedicated machine.

Server GC creates one heap and one GC thread per core and collects in parallel, giving more throughput and shorter pauses on big heaps, but it uses more memory (often 2 to 3 times) and is a poor choice for small containers with 1 core or for desktop apps. Workstation GC suits client apps. Enable it with <ServerGarbageCollector>true</ServerGarbageCollector> and measure.

code.title: Async cache: one shared load per key, failures evicted

followUps:
Store the last access time with each entry and, on every read, check whether now - lastAccess exceeds the window; if it does, treat the entry as expired, otherwise update the time.

if (e.LastAccess + ttl < now) { map.TryRemove(key, out _); return Miss; }
e.LastAccess = now;   // slide the window
return e.Value;

Add an absolute maximum age too, or a popular entry would never expire and could serve stale data forever. A background sweep removes entries nobody asks for again.

Each instance has its own copy, so after one instance updates the data the other keeps serving the old value until its entry expires.

Example: instance A changes a price from 10 to 12 and invalidates its cache, but instance B still shows 10 for up to the TTL (say 5 minutes). Fixes: a shared cache such as Redis, or a small local L1 with a short TTL plus invalidation messages over pub/sub. Also each instance loads the same key once, so N instances make N loads at startup.

code.title: ArrayPool Rent and Return with try/finally

followUps:
Because the pool hands out arrays in fixed size buckets (powers of two such as 16, 32, 64 ... elements), so a request for 100 elements returns a 128-element array.

This makes returned arrays reusable by later callers asking for similar sizes, instead of keeping thousands of exact sizes. The consequence is that you must track your own length and never use array.Length, or you would process 28 garbage items.

stackalloc is safe for small, bounded sizes that you control, and when assigned to a Span<T> so it cannot escape the method.

Span<byte> buf = n <= 256 ? stackalloc byte[n] : new byte[n];

The stack is about 1 MB per thread (8 MB on some Linux setups), so a size taken from user input can cause a stack overflow that kills the process. Keep it under about 1 KB, fall back to ArrayPool for bigger sizes, and never return it.

It tells the compiler to stop warning: it says "trust me, this is not null" and does nothing at run time, so a null still crashes later with a NullReferenceException.

With string? s = Find(); int n = s!.Length; the compiler is quiet, but if Find() returned null you get the exception on that line. Use it only where you know something the compiler cannot, such as after a framework-guaranteed initialisation, and prefer a null check, [NotNullWhen] or a fix to the design.

A required member must be set in an object initializer, and the compiler then treats it as initialised, so a non-nullable property needs no constructor to avoid the warning.

class User { public required string Name { get; init; } }
var u = new User { Name = "Ann" };   // ok
var v = new User();                   // error: Name is required

It removes the "uninitialised non-nullable property" warning without making the property nullable or using = null!. It is still only compile-time: serializers and reflection can bypass it.

code.title: Type patterns over a closed outcome hierarchy

followUps:
The compiler checks that every possible value is handled by tracking the types or constants it knows about; if a case is missing it gives a warning, not an error.

With a sealed or abstract hierarchy C# cannot know that no one will add another subclass elsewhere, so a switch over Outcome that handles Paid and Declined will warn about missing patterns, and you need a _ branch or a throw. Enums and bool are exhaustive; for hierarchies people simulate closed types with a private constructor and a final _ => throw arm.

A slice pattern .. inside a list pattern matches any number of elements, including zero, and may capture them as a subarray or sublist.

int[] a = { 1, 2, 3, 4 };
if (a is [1, .. var middle, 4])   // middle = { 2, 3 }
    Console.WriteLine(middle.Length);   // 2

Only one .. is allowed per list pattern. [var first, ..] means at least one element, and [.., var last] reads the last element without indexing.

Records are the most misused, because people apply them to everything, including entities that have identity and mutable state.

Example: an Order record with a changing status compares equal to another order with the same fields, and a record with a List member is only shallowly immutable. A close second is LINQ and async inside hot loops. Use records for data transfer and value-like objects, and plain classes for things with identity (an order with an id is the same order even when its status changes).

Code is hot enough when a profiler or benchmark shows it consuming a large share of the time (say 10 percent or more of a request) and the gain would be visible to users or cost.

Steps: measure with a profiler or BenchmarkDotNet, find the top few methods, estimate the gain (a method taking 2 percent of the time can save at most 2 percent), change one thing and measure again. If a request takes 100 ms and 95 ms is the database, rewriting the 1 ms loop is wasted effort; fix the query first.
